newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian experts raise issues of air safety in India.
newsitem.headline: Asian experts raise issues of air safety in India.

text.p: Asian aviation experts on Wednesday questioned standards of air safety in the Indian subcontinent in the wake of an air disaster that killed some 350 people.
But many experts said it was premature to jump to conclusions on what caused Tuesday's mid-air collision between a Saudi Arabian Boeing 747 jet and a Kazakhstan Ilyushin cargo plane.

"Safety standards in India, Bangladesh and Nepal are very low and should be radically improved. We often find it irritating when we enter the air space of these countries. People at the control towers fumble," said a senior official responsible for flight safety of Bangladesh airline Biman.
Most airlines have long taken extra care over Indian air space because of its "low traffic control standard", said a flight safety officer with an Asian airline based in Bangkok.

"Most Indian air safety monitor personnel are not sufficiently trained nor qualified to handle their jobs. They sometimes gave two airlines the same flight ceiling instructions at the same time that could cause a collision," she said.

An air accident investigator based in Singapore, who declined to be identified, said it was common practice for flight crews in Indian sub-continent air space to supplement radar navigation by looking out of the windows.
"Aircrews are constantly carrying out a visual watch because they are uneasy with the general standard of air traffic control and equipment across the Indian sub-continent," he said.

The Indian subcontinent, a corridor for flights between Europe and South East Asia/Australia, does not have total radar coverage in its air space, industry sources said. But Tuesday's accident was near New Delhi airport which had radar coverage.

"Obviously, the crash raises all the normal concerns about air safety. Mid-air collisons are extremely rare. In this particular case...the reasons as to why the two airlines collided in mid-air one can only speculate on," said Richard Stirland, director general of Orient Airlines Association (OAA) based in Manila.
He said the New Dehli airport, in terms of arrivals and departures, was not busier than other major airports in Asia such as Singapore, Hong Kong and Bangkok.

"Based on my knowledge of the traffic in India and the normal level of efficiency at New Dehli, it would be wrong to say at this stage that the accident was a result of the airport being too busy or there was too much traffic," said Stirland.
Several pilots told Reuters a possible cause for the collision could be human error from either the traffic control side or from one of the pilots involved.
Japanese air traffice expert Eiichiro Sekigawa said there could have been a communications breakdown at the handover zone between the control tower and the air flight path control system.
"The collision happened just at the point where control tower air traffic control ends and flight path air traffic control begins... It could be that a sloppy handover caused the accident," he said.
Sekigawa also said a communication failure between pilots and air traffic control could be the cause.

A pilot with Singapore Airlines who declined to be identified said: "There are many factors here, it could be the air traffic control side, the two pilots or even a mechanical failure in equipment. It would be unfair to say at this time what is the cause."

Expressing similar sentiments, OAA's Stirland said: "The (July) TWA accident is a perfect example where people have shot their mouths off on what may or may not have caused the accident. I think it is really to early to speculate on the reasons for the crash."
In July this year, TWA flight 800 exploded in a fireball over the Atlantic Ocean after taking off from Kennedy Airport, New York, en route for Paris. The cause has yet to be determined.
